In Support of LD 2026: "An Act Regarding Distributions from the Stipend Fund for Agricultural Fair Competitions and Events"
Honorable members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry, I am Bill Pluecker, and I represent House District 44, comprising the towns of Warren, Hope and Union.
Thank you for the opportunity to speak to you today in support of this legislation, which addresses a practical challenge facing Maine's agricultural fairs. Currently, stipend distributions only apply to competitions judged during official fair dates. This technical restriction creates real operational problems for fair organizers across our state.
Maine's agricultural fairs are community institutions that celebrate our farming heritage and bring neighbors together. However, the current system forces all judging to occur during the fair itself, when volunteers and staff are stretched thin managing crowds, vendors, and countless activities. This bill would allow judging to begin up to twenty-four hours before official fair dates while still qualifying for stipend distributions.
By spreading judging across additional hours reduces bottlenecks and ensures careful, thorough evaluation of livestock, produce, and crafts. Exhibitors and fairgoers can see winning entries from opening day, enhancing their experience and recognizing participants sooner. And perhaps most importantly, judges can volunteer in other essential capacities during the fair--working gates, assisting with youth programs, or supporting wherever help is needed.
Our agricultural fairs operate on tight budgets and depend heavily on volunteers. This modest change gives fair boards crucial flexibility without additional state expense. The emergency preamble ensures implementation for this year's fair season, when organizers are already finalizing schedules.
I urge this Committee's support for Maine's agricultural fairs and the thousands of volunteers who make them possible. Thank you.

District 44: Hope, Union, & Warren

Good afternoon, Senator Talbot-Ross, Representative Pluecker, and distinguished members of the Agricultural, Conservation and Forestry Committee. My name is Darlene
Newcombe, I am the Superintendent and a Trustee of Windsor Fair.
Today I am here to testify in favor of LD 2026. As one of Maines larger fairs we take in over
1500 items into the exhibition hall. The work to accomplish this takes many hands and many hours. The crew at the exhibition Hall starts on the Monday before the fair setting up
and organizes to receive items to be exhibited. We work 10 hour days on Tuesday and
Wednesday helping the public fill out papen/vork for their items proceeded by processing and entering into the computer system. Thursday has always been about a 10-hour day working with thejudges to be sure everything was examined and ribboned. Friday has in the past been used for decorating and displaying items for the public viewing. As you can see when you have these many items it is a long process to accomplish.
if we were to judge duringthe fair, we would have to close our doors during the first day and at least half of the second day to accomplish all that we need to do. Our fairgoers would be upset if they were not able to enter the hall on the opening day of the fair. if we were to judge, decorate and display items while the exhibition hall doors are open, we would need
to be concerned about the safety of our fairgoers and the safety of the items to be exhibited. This would not lend for a good experience for our fairgoers and volunteers.
Also, we are trying to work in several contests and activities during the week. We have
several demonstrators, such as rug hookers, spinners, felters, oyster farms, bakers, and
general crafters that come in to talk with fairgoers regarding their crafts. Judging during fair
hours would cut back on the time available to bringthese talented people to the public.
As you can see our 10 days are consumed with many activities while also trying to keep a
clean, organized and safe environment for the public.
The ability tojudge and receive stipend dollars before our fair opens would be a real help to Windsor Fair.
Thank you for your time. I will make myself available for the work session.
Respectfully submitted,
Darlene Newcombe

Judy Taylor Gagnon Cumberland County Fair LD 2026
Good afternoon, Senator Talbot-Ross, Representative Pluecker and distinguished members of the Agricultural, Conservation and Forestry Committee. My name is Judy Taylor Gagnon and I am a member of the Cumberlan County Fair and a staff member of the Cumberland Fair Exhibition Hall. I am here today to testify in favor of LD 2026, representing the Superintendents of the Exhibition Hall of Cumberland County Fair, Carolyn Small and Lynn Copp. We are concerned about, as are many other Exhibition Hall Superintendents, the ruling that judging of the contests should be during the fair times for the following reasons: 1. Last year we had 2,396 items to be judged, ribboned and displayed. At only one minute each to judge, that is over almost 40 hours of time. That's why we need two days for the 24 judges that work for us. Losing two days of our seven-day Fair would be devastating. 2. Safety is a great concern. If judging is done with fairgoers coming through the Hall at the same time, a traffic flow danger is created. Also, with the staff attempting to creatively and safely display entries after they have been judged, teetering around on ladders and the display of shelves with visitors coming through, another safety issue is created. 3. Next is the security of entries. How do we protect the entries if they are on tables in the aisles while they are being judged while visitors are passing through? If entries are on the tables to be judged, they are then at risk of being unprotected with the possibilty of being stolen or damaged. If fairgoers are viewing them, there is the hazard of spills or greasy fingers touching things or powdered sugar falling on them. If drinks are spilled on photographs, paper crafts or watercolor paintngs, they are completely ruined. 4. Should the entries be on display before being judged? How can they then be examined thrououghly? Quilts hanging up cannot be properly assessed from the floor. 5. Anonymity for most of the judges is a significant element. Provocation, hassling and aggressive questions are big concerns here. If an entrant should happen to be present while their entry is being judged, they could question the judgement. Distraction is another issue for the judges. If they have to answer questions while they are judging, they cannot focus on the job at hand, and that increases the demand and pressure of their time. 6. We use our tables to place entries on while the judges are working. As each item is judged, members of our staff then attach the ribbon and put the ribboned items in the display areas. Afer all the judging is completed, the tables are then put in place for our demos. So, do we display the items first for the judges to not be able to accurately and meticulously do the job, or do we use the tables, as we have forever done, and lose two days of people doing demos for us? The demo folks are all willing to interact with and educate visitors about their crafts, so losing any days is counter-productive. We at the Fairs are supposed to be the promoters, educators, advocates and supporters of Maine agriculture, and we are being stifled in doing are job appropriately. 7. There are other events and entries at Cumberland Fair that are judged during the fair. The giant pumpkin/squash contest, judging of fresh fruits and vegetables done by the State of Maine Horiculturist, the whoopie pie contest, the decorated and tasting cupcake contest, and the State of Maine Two Crusted Apple Pie contest are all judged during the week; thus, we are compliant with this ruling with those events. 8. The definition of exhibition is displaying, showing, presenting and demonstrating. Nowhere in that definition does judging exist. 9. While the 24-hour factor being proposed by LD 2026 is certainly helpful, it still lacks enough time for our jobs to be done comprehensively. Our ultimate hope is that you will see these concerns and build an allowance for the exhibition halls at Maine fairs to do their judging in the days prior to their Fair opening.

Yours very sincerely from the Cumberland Fair Exhibition Hall, Carolyn Small, Superintendent csmall1943@maine.rr.com Lynn Blanchette Copp, Assistent Superintendent lynncopp@msn.com Judy Taylor Gagnon, Exhibition Hall Staff Member jetg1022@gmail.com
